    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that after a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.
    • After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.
    • The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that after a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal. The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map. Expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. As in that title, in GTA VI, the natural world is more than just a backdrop for the main story: Side quests like alligator hunting and a zoologist challenge lead players into the great outdoors. Players have eagerly anticipated the wildlife. A promotional image featuring a lionfish—an invasive species in Florida—sparked hopeful discussion about spear hunting, which is one of the methods used to control their population. Other fans kept running lists of species confirmed ahead of the release date. GTA VI’s birding gameplay and inclusion of 62 avian species has been a particular source of buzz online, and hobbyists are already logging the species they spy on a dedicated website called Leonida Birds. One person said that playing Red Dead Redemption 2 had “flipped the birding switch on,” and that they’ve since identified birds from the game in real life. Perhaps unsurprisingly, research suggests that this deep immersion in video game environments can serve as a valuable way to communicate information about the real natural world, including a study in which RDR2 players correctly identified more photos of wildlife species that had appeared in the game than non-players. “Not sure how GTA VI has suddenly turned me into David Attenborough,” one player remarked on X, “but I just logged off an 8 hour session and immediately want to hop back on to study more birds and wildlife.” In a study published in Geoscience Communication this week, researchers used GTA V’s digital replication of Los Angeles—coupled with data like Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projections and records of past flooding—to simulate floods caused by sea level rise. Paul Nörenberg, one of the researchers, said in a press release that engaging with these climate effects in a familiar landscape “can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.” Another study, which interviewed gamers about their experiences, observed that different games allow participants to explore nature through different contexts and perspectives, and games that include environmental destruction “made them contend with exploiting and subjugating nature—both in-game and in the actual world.” Though Grand Theft Auto’s plots are designed to let players explore a life of crime—not climate disaster—the latest installment’s gameplay does weave in a range of real-world environmental topics, from animal conservation to chemicals in agriculture. One mission centers on the exotic animal trade; another involves freeing an orca from the Vice City Oceanarium, likely a reference to the now-shuttered Miami Seaquarium, which faced criticism for owning an orca named Lolita that died in captivity in 2023. In a third, a strawberry grower asks the player to visit a meth lab to pick up “discontinued” chemicals that he sprays on his unnaturally large crops, according to an IGN walk-through. This also echoes reality. Driscoll’s, a major agribusiness, faces a class-action lawsuit that alleges the company sold strawberries contaminated with harmful chemicals without disclosing them. Video game realism does have its limits: The real-life strawberries haven’t turned anyone into giant mutants. Yet.

    After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.

    The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map.

    Expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. As in that title, in GTA VI, the natural world is more than just a backdrop for the main story: Side quests like alligator hunting and a zoologist challenge lead players into the great outdoors.

    Recent findings suggest that players have eagerly anticipated the wildlife. A promotional image featuring a lionfish—an invasive species in Florida—sparked hopeful discussion about spear hunting, which is one of the methods used to control their population. Other fans kept running lists of species confirmed ahead of the release date.

    It has been revealed that GTA VI’s birding gameplay and inclusion of 62 avian species has been a particular source of buzz online, and hobbyists are already logging the species they spy on a dedicated website called Leonida Birds. One person noted that playing Red Dead Redemption 2 had “flipped the birding switch on,” and that they’ve since identified birds from the game in real life.

    Perhaps unsurprisingly, research suggests that this deep immersion in video game environments can serve as a valuable way to communicate information about the real natural world, including a study in which RDR2 players correctly identified more photos of wildlife species that had appeared in the game than non-players.

    “Not sure how GTA VI has suddenly turned me into David Attenborough,” one player remarked on X, “but I just logged off an 8 hour session and immediately want to hop back on to study more birds and wildlife.”.

    In a study published in Geoscience Communication this week, researchers used GTA V’s digital replication of Los Angeles—coupled with data like Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projections and records of past flooding—to simulate floods caused by sea level rise.

    Paul Nörenberg, one of the researchers, said in a press release that engaging with these climate effects in a familiar landscape “can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.”.

    Another study, which interviewed gamers about their experiences, observed that different games allow participants to explore nature through different contexts and perspectives, and games that include environmental destruction “made them contend with exploiting and subjugating nature—both in-game and in the actual world.”.

    Though Grand Theft Auto’s plots are designed to let players explore a life of crime—not climate disaster—the upcoming installment’s gameplay does weave in a range of real-world environmental topics, from animal conservation to chemicals in agriculture.

    One mission centers on the exotic animal trade; another involves freeing an orca from the Vice City Oceanarium, likely a reference to the now-shuttered Miami Seaquarium, which faced criticism for owning an orca named Lolita that died in captivity in 2023.

    In a third, a strawberry grower asks the player to visit a meth lab to pick up “discontinued” chemicals that he sprays on his unnaturally large crops, according to an IGN walk-through. This also echoes reality. Driscoll’s, a major agribusiness, faces a class-action lawsuit that alleges the manufacturer sold strawberries contaminated with harmful chemicals without disclosing them.

    It has been revealed that video game realism does have its limits: The real-life strawberries haven’t turned anyone into giant mutants. Yet.

    #92902. Latest Update: 11 career decisions high performers regret making too late

    Latest Update: 11 career decisions high performers regret making too late

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed.
    • In a recent development, some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed.
    • The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the manufacturer.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed. The following insights, from experts in the field, reveal which moves high performers often wish they had made sooner, from protecting their health to asking for help and building stronger networks. These lessons offer clear steps for making better choices before regret sets in. Delegate Authority While Capacity Remains The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the company. When I founded my first Scandinavian fine jewelry brand in Oslo at 22, I built our early momentum by personally touching every single bottleneck: approving every creative cut, negotiating every creator seeding deal, and rewriting campaign copy at 2:00 a.m. Because revenue was climbing and we were landing cultural placements like Khaby Lame and Vogue Scandinavia, I mistook exhaustion for leverage. The turning point came when I realized that by being the best operator in the room, I had capped the company’s valuation at the limit of my personal nervous system. High performers wait until they hit burnout to build standard operating procedures and delegate authority, whereas you actually have to hand off the keys while you still have 40% left in the tank. Once I forced myself to step out of daily order orchestration and document our visual and distribution protocols so the business ran without my fingerprints on every transaction, two things happened: Our enterprise value became transferable (allowing us to close a clean private acquisition exit in Q4 2024), and my own bandwidth opened up to direct film productions. If I could go back, I would have documented and delegated my favorite tasks 12 months earlier, not just the chores I hated. Mommi Live, founder, managing partner & creative director, Mommi Limited Archive Evidence Beyond External Platforms Keeping their track record inside someone else’s platform. High performers usually build their reputation where the work happens: an employer’s system, a marketplace profile, a client’s internal tools. It feels like the record will always be there. Then the job ends, the platform changes its rules, or the old proof simply stops being shown, and years of results are hard to point to. I learned this with my own business. I started selling video editing on Fiverr in 2020, while I was studying computer science. That grew into Mark Studios, which has completed more than 8,000 orders and earned 4,500+ reviews, with a 4.9 rating and Top Rated status. But Fiverr only indicates roughly the last two years of reviews, so the visible proof of the early years keeps shrinking even as the total grows. The work was real. The evidence just lived somewhere I didn’t control. What I’d do differently, and what I tell anyone doing great work inside a company or a platform: Keep your own record from day one. Write a short case study after every project that matters, with the problem, what you did, and a measurable result. For a channel whose thumbnails and titles we’ve handled since August 2025, VidIQ showed views up 30.1% week over week when we captured the stats in May. That number now sits in a case study on my own website instead of only in a client conversation. Ask for testimonials you’re allowed to reuse, and save the numbers while they’re fresh. Your reputation is an asset. Make sure you hold a copy of it. Mark Santos, founder & creative director, Mark Studios LLC Ask for Help Before Depletion The decision I see high performers regret most isn’t burning out. It’s waiting until they’re depleted to ask for help, because by then the choice is already gone. Their body makes it for them. I’m a licensed counselor supervisor and president of a South Carolina practice with more than 60 therapists across 10 offices, plus online therapy. I watch this play out in my own field constantly. The strongest clinicians I supervise are usually the last ones to bring a hard case to supervision. Asking feels like admitting they can’t handle it, and they’ve built their whole identity around being the person others lean on. So they carry it quietly. And it doesn’t show up right away. It shows up months later as irritability, or dread on Sunday nights, or a sudden wish to quit work they used to love. What I tell them is pretty straightforward. Build the support in while things are still going well. Put a standing check-in on the calendar with a supervisor, a mentor, or a therapist before there’s anything urgent to report. When I started my practice with my husband, David, in 2019, I learned fast that the same logic applies to running a company. Support that you set up early costs you maybe an hour a week. Support that you set up late costs you a year of recovery. The best time to ask for help is when you don’t feel like you need it yet. Kenza Haddock, president, Oceanic Counseling Group Broadcast Accomplishments to Gain Advocacy High performers are great at getting things done, often to the detriment of their career progression. If you’re so busy taking care of things, then communicating out what you’re accomplishing is often the last thing on your list. That’s either because you don’t want to brag, or you assume others know what you’re working on. Not learning to communicate up and out is often a regret. I’ve worked with a senior leader whose manager was let go. They established relationships with their new manager and also with other senior leaders in the organization. They learned to communicate regularly as a part of their role to inform the what and the why of their accomplishments through one reorg after another. When yet another manager was let go, they were promoted into the role due to the awareness and extended support they’d built. I’m now working with a younger employee with a new manager on how to own their weekly reporting, proactively communicating to the team what their weekly accomplishments are and how these fit into the greater goals. People can only advocate for you if they can say what you actually do. High performers often learn this alternate side of their role far too late. Dana Zellers, executive & leadership coach, team facilitator, Dana Zellers Own Your Professional Future I’ve talked with more than a thousand executives in the past four years and the biggest regrets that I hear from high performers is relying on their employers to take care of them instead of taking ownership for their career decisions. I have had more clients than I can count who worked for Fortune 100 employers for 20+ years. They believed that they would retire with that company, but then the business changed, they lost their job, and they were left trying to figure out where to go next. No matter where you are in your career, you need to remember that companies are usually going to look out for themselves first. You need to plan your career accordingly. “Job hugging” has been the newest trend, where workers hang on to jobs that they don’t necessarily love. Sure, there is risk in leaving your job, but there is also risk at staying in your current job, especially if layoffs are on the horizon. Staying open to potential opportunities, both actively through networking and passively through an optimized LinkedIn profile, is key to building a career that lasts. Colleen Paulson, executive career consultant, Ageless Careers Align Ambition With Desired Work One decision high performers often make too late is to actively manage their careers rather than assuming that success in their current jobs will take care of that for them. Excelling at your job and managing your career are related, but they’re not the same thing. I’ve seen this play out in two ways. First, high performers become exceptionally good at identifying what it takes to succeed within their organizations. They earn promotions, navigate politics, and build expertise and relationships. But they don’t always stop to ask whether what they’re building is what they actually want. Over the last few years, I’ve worked with leaders who realized that the roles they’d spent years working toward had taken them further away from the work they loved, whether that’s working directly with clients or coaching their teams. We often think about the title and impact, but not the altitude we’ll have to lead at. A promotion often means moving away from doing the work yourself to creating the conditions for others to do it, through strategy, resource allocation, and management. That’s a very different job. Second, high performers forget to build career optionality before they need it. They invest heavily in building skills, relationships, and credibility within their organizations. That’s important, but incomplete. Internal recognition matters, but so does building an external professional network. Think of it as a savings account you’re contributing to over time. Too often, I’ve coached leaders who gave everything to their organizations, sometimes staying for more than a decade, only to find themselves facing a layoff, burnout, or a desire to pivot—and realizing they had limited external networks and little understanding of how their skills would translate elsewhere. A few simple ways to avoid these traps: • Before pursuing a promotion, talk to people already in the role. Understand what their day-to-day looks like, what they’ve had to give up, and what success actually requires. • While you’re happily employed, invest in relationships outside your organization and learn about other industries. Volunteer opportunities and nonprofit board service can be excellent ways to do this while also giving back. • The goal is not to constantly be on a job hunt. It’s to make sure you’re building a career that reflects what you want, with the flexibility to make different choices along the way. Lisa Friscia, president and founder, Franca Consulting Pursue Ventures Through Small Bets One decision high performers often regret making too late is waiting to act on an entrepreneurial idea because it feels safer to stay on secure footing. With more responsibility, high performers can get attached to income or get sucked into “golden handcuffs.” They’re less likely to leave for a more enjoyable job or take a risk at starting something up. I have seen this with seasoned corporate leaders who had a viable concept for years, but once they were settled with a mortgage, family responsibilities, and a stable role, the leap started to feel like too much to lose. The regret often sharpens when they later watch someone else succeed with a similar idea, because possibility suddenly looks like proof that they could have moved earlier. What could have been done differently is keeping the risk muscle active through small, regular bets while still employed, such as testing the idea in low-stakes ways and building comfort with uncertainty. That approach reduces the gap between the idea and bringing it to market, so the decision is not one major, intimidating jump. Also, it’s important to have accountability partners who ask us hard questions or challenge the status quo related to our experience, comfort, and career. How much money is enough? When is the right time? I hear high performers regret missed opportunities with a radical role departure or a job abroad or starting something new, going back to school when they were younger. We feel guilted or bullied into the norm by our families, peers, neighbors and society to do the “right” and “responsible” thing, then later wish we had taken the road less traveled or taken a risk. Janice Perkins, executive coach, Janice Perkins Restore Health Through Daily Habits The one decision high performers often regret is not focusing on their health and well-being as a function of improving their daily performance. All too often, high performers have had success all of their lives. They create habits in their 20s when their energy levels are high and their body can bounce back relatively promptly. As they start to advance their career in their 30s, 40s, and 50s, these high performers continue with these same habits, focusing only on work. Working late, missing sleep, skipping meals, and perhaps drinking alcohol (even in moderate amounts) drain more and more energy, physical and mental, from their daily output. To these habits, they add coffee to wake up and sugar intake to combat the energy crashes. This leads to poor sleep, and the cycle continues every day. It is possible to reverse these bad habits with small intentional changes in one’s daily lifestyle. A couple of simple examples are arising at the same time every day, including weekends, and getting morning daylight within the first 60-120 minutes of waking up. Steve Fiore, executive performance advisor, Rooted in Curiosity Serve Your Network Regularly As a career coach, I usually connect with high performers when they are in the midst of, or planning for, a transition. The #1 regret I hear is that leaders feel they lost touch with their network while building their careers. They understandably hesitate to make an ask when they haven’t connected in three, five, or even 10+ years. It can feel cringey and awkward reaching out when so much time has passed. But now more than ever, your network is your career net worth. So I hope more high achievers keep that in mind. The easiest way to keep in touch with your network? Be a helper. Haley McNeel Drake, résumé writer & career coach, The Career Revisory Exit Places That Diminish Your Worth One important decision I’ve seen time and time again among high performers is not leaving an organization sooner when their value went unrecognized. Being a high performer doesn’t automatically translate to timely promotions or special accolades for great work. In the pursuit of success, a high performer can work to increase their visibility and yet those efforts don’t lead to a promotion. Not because they’re doing anything wrong or focused on things that won’t get them noticed, but because of office politics or favoritism. What people often overlook and hate to admit is that you simply may be in the wrong environment where no matter what you do, your value will be unrecognized. For high performers, staying too long in an environment after making efforts to be “promotion ready” will eventually catch up, once they end up in an environment where they are valued, appreciated, and recognized for their work. Owning your competence, knowing your value, and being honest with yourself is part of high performance. Not getting a promotion the first time you ask for one isn’t necessarily a sign that you need to start looking or you’re being undervalued. However, the challenge arises when the same cycle repeats, and you’re getting empty promises instead of a kept word. Pay attention to nuance, yes: changes in the broader organization, natural attrition, etc. Timing is everything. But also, give yourself a timeline. If the opportunities you want to pursue don’t become available within that timeline, and those in charge can’t give you a blueprint to help you get where you want to be, you then make a different decision. And that could be planning your exit. Lisa De Nicola, leadership & executive coach; founder, HER Lead; Lisa De Nicola Broaden Expertise Outside Familiar Functions One decision high performers often make too late is stepping outside the area where they’ve already proven themselves. When you’re good at something, you tend to get more of it. You get promoted, take on bigger responsibilities, and become the person everyone relies on. That’s great for your career, but it can also keep you in a fairly narrow lane. Earlier in my career at HD Supply, I spent time working directly with branch managers, and one thing I did was lead financial literacy sessions. These were for people making decisions every day about pricing, inventory, customers, and how to run their businesses. I learned a tremendous amount from those conversations. They helped me understand the operating decisions behind the financial results, and that made me a much better finance leader. Looking back, I would have sought out more of that exposure earlier rather than waiting for opportunities to come through my formal responsibilities. My advice to high performers is to take on something outside your comfort zone before you feel completely ready. Spend time with customers, get involved in operations, or volunteer for a project that forces you to learn another part of the business. Being really good at your current job gets you noticed. Understanding how the whole business works prepares you for the next one. Thomas DeFabrizio, CFO, Vertage.

    Recent findings suggest that pay attention to nuance, yes: changes in the broader organization, natural attrition, etc. Timing is everything. But also, give yourself a timeline. If the opportunities you want to pursue don’t become available within that timeline, and those in charge can’t give you a blueprint to help you get where you want to be, you then make a different decision. And that could be planning your exit.

    Lisa De Nicola, leadership & executive coach; founder, HER Lead; Lisa De Nicola.

    One decision high performers often make too late is stepping outside the area where they’ve already proven themselves.

    When you’re good at something, you tend to get more of it. You get promoted, take on bigger responsibilities, and become the person everyone relies on. That’s great for your career, but it can also keep you in a fairly narrow lane.

    Industry observers note that earlier in my career at HD Supply, I spent time working directly with branch managers, and one thing I did was lead financial literacy sessions. These were for people making decisions every day about pricing, inventory, customers, and how to run their businesses.

    Industry observers note that I learned a tremendous amount from those conversations. They helped me understand the operating decisions behind the financial results, and that made me a much better finance leader.

    Looking back, I would have sought out more of that exposure earlier rather than waiting for opportunities to come through my formal responsibilities.

    My advice to high performers is to take on something outside your comfort zone before you feel completely ready. Spend time with customers, get involved in operations, or volunteer for a project that forces you to learn another part of the business.

    Recent findings suggest that being really good at your current job gets you noticed. Understanding how the whole business works prepares you for the next one.

    Thomas DeFabrizio, CFO, Vertage.

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
    • In a recent development, every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan.
    • Recent findings suggest that so what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    Sources indicate that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

    7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

    In a recent development, every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest upgrade from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

    Recent findings suggest that so what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

    In a recent development, today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

    Where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the newly introduced limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

    A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

    Sources indicate that shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

    Industry observers note that another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice quickly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

    Industry observers note that for most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows quickly.

    It has been revealed that the safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

    It has been revealed that an expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

    The damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

    Sources indicate that nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

    It has been revealed that automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:.

    Look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

    What closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

    For each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the glitch date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

    Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

    Industry observers note that most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

    Here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

    The fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

    The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:.

    Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

    If you’d like a second pair of eyes on your certificates, you can start a 30-day free trial of Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring.

    #92898. VAST states petabyte SSDs will outgrow today’s parallel file system RAID

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1392 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

    VAST states petabyte SSDs will outgrow today’s parallel file system RAID

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1392 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • VAST Data says petabyte SSDs will outgrow RAID in today’s parallel file systems, according to a simulation of its own 900 PB system that puts the odds of data loss at 1 in 11 over 10 years.
    • Bigger drives take longer to rebuild after a failure, leaving more time for further failures to lose data, but operators will still want those large drives because many sites are power-constrained and storage power scales with bandwidth rather than capacity.
    • Sources indicate that the manufacturer’s principal technical strategist, Glenn Lockwood, walked through the simulation, described as a “discrete event simulation” using real failure data, in an Exhibitor Forum talk during SC26’s HPC System Hardware and Architecture session.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    VAST Data says petabyte SSDs will outgrow RAID in today’s parallel file systems, according to a simulation of its own 900 PB system that puts the odds of data loss at 1 in 11 over 10 years. At Supercomputing 2026 (SC26), the organization explains how.

    Bigger drives take longer to rebuild after a failure, leaving more time for further failures to lose data, but operators will still want those large drives because many sites are power-constrained and storage power scales with bandwidth rather than capacity. VAST’s recommended fix: system-wide erasure coding with at least three parity strips.

    Sources indicate that the manufacturer’s principal technical strategist, Glenn Lockwood, walked through the simulation, described as a “discrete event simulation” using real failure data, in an Exhibitor Forum talk during SC26’s HPC System Hardware and Architecture session. With petabyte-scale SSDs swapped in, enclosure-local declustered RAID — the approach used by DDN EXAScaler and HPE Cray ClusterStor, per Lockwood — has those exceptionally high odds of data loss. With global declustering and extra parity, operators can get this down to 1 in 54 million, a significant improvement, but VAST’s own scheme gets to about 1 in 62 billion, three orders of magnitude better.

    In a recent development, lockwood’s case for petabyte SSDs rests on how storage power scales: at about 28 W per SSD, regardless of capacity and including its share of the surrounding infrastructure, plus 20 W per GB/s of bandwidth. Getting 900 PB of flash from 15 TB SSDs would take more than 63K drives, each adding its own bandwidth, for 190 TB/s at 5.6 MW, or “the equivalent of 3,100 or so of Blackwell Ultra GPUs.” Lockwood notes, though, that “real AI applications in our experience have never approached needing anything close to that level of performance” from the storage.

    It has been revealed that with 122 TB drives, at almost an 8K count and much lower 8 TB/s of aggregate bandwidth, the power draw is less than a tenth of that, at about 400 kW. Within that budget, 15 TB SSDs top out at about 250 PB, even with no power left for performance. That power could be better spent on compute and, anyway, 245 TB-class drives are already arriving, with much larger drives expected.

    Everything is a series of trade-offs, though, and larger drives come with their own caveats. Lockwood acknowledges the usual reaction to a 245 TB drive: that it’s “a major blast radius,” since a single failure leaves much more to rebuild. And it does take longer: at the same per-drive speed, a 122 TB drive takes twice as long to rebuild as a 60 TB drive, leaving a longer window in which a second failure in a traditional RAID 5 set loses data. Per-drive capacity is potentially outpacing bandwidth increases and, at least within a generation, “the performance of each individual drive does not change,” so this is something that must be accepted or overcome.

    It has been revealed that the simulated system involves 7,920 SSDs at 122 TB each, using 180 enclosures with 44 drives each. With a RAID 5 single parity solution, there is a 100% chance of data loss over 10 years, but “no one uses single parity anymore.” Double parity still has 1 in 150 odds of data loss over a decade and is considered “state of the art for many open source file systems,” and he explicitly names Lustre and BeeGFS within this context.

    Industry observers note that for proprietary parallel file system implementations, declustered RAID within an enclosure is the state of the art, instead. Declustered RAID spreads each drive group’s data, parity, and spare space over more drives than usual, allowing for faster rebuilds. Keeping it within an enclosure means that the spread still stays within a single box of drives. Swapping petabyte SSDs into that enclosure-level declustering is what gets to the headline 1 in 11 odds of data loss.

    As for the mentioned rivals, DDN’s DCR, in one published configuration, uses RAID 6 in an 8+2 array for a 24-NVMe SSD pool. That means eight data strips plus two parity strips per stripe, allowing any two drives in the pool to fail without losing data, and each stripe is spread over 10 of the 24 drives. DDN has conceded in the past that larger systems may need more than DCR. HPE’s declustered RAID solution is known as GridRAID, with declustered parity per enclosure half, meaning two 12-drive pools per 24-drive enclosure.

    Perlmutter, the supercomputer at Berkeley Lab’s National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center, where Lockwood once worked, used GridRAID with 8+2+1 RAID 6 per 12-drive object storage target, Lustre’s name for a storage unit. The +1 is one spare drive’s worth of space, spread across all 12, so a rebuild writes to every surviving drive rather than to a single replacement. Either way, protection stops at two failures in a pool of one or two dozen drives, and only those drives can assist with a rebuild. This is the scenario in VAST’s simulation with the catastrophic failure rate.

    Odds of data loss over 10 years.

    Open-source Lustre and BeeGFS, typically.

    Declustered RAID within an enclosure.

    DDN EXAScaler, HPE Cray ClusterStor.

    Declustered RAID across the whole system, plus extra parity.

    VAST’s own scheme (not detailed).

    It has been revealed that several solutions exist, with limits. Adding a parity strip for triple parity reduces the odds of data loss. Global declustering, on its own, can also reduce the odds a little bit, with faster rebuild times. However, stripes are spread over every drive in the cluster, so two random failures are more likely to hit the same stripe, meaning a larger fault domain.

    In a recent development, if both approaches are used, which is the minimum bar for him, you get down to getting struck by “lightning on your birthday” odds. VAST already publishes quadruple parity, which is beyond this bar. Using VAST’s own “special magic,” undisclosed but beyond the minimum bar, drops the odds even further, specifically for the petabyte SSDs, which is the real target of the talk.

    It has been revealed that then we get to the metadata, the data about data, which in this case is the index of where every piece of every file dwells. Every write necessarily updates it synchronously, so VAST keeps it on separate, fast SSDs as three full copies for replication, not parity. This means it can survive two failures, which is less than the data’s four parity strips, and the index becomes the weakest link. With 122 TB drives, he puts the data drives’ odds at 1 in 78 trillion over 10 years, against 1 in 58 million for metadata. To Lockwood, this illustrates that the surrounding infrastructure is the real risk, given the failure gap between the index and regular data.

    Industry observers note that rebuilding in the index area starts about 12 seconds after a failure, on average, versus about two minutes for data drives, Lockwood says. VAST’s procedure more generally, for when a drive drops out, is to power-cycle it and hope, so there is always some delay before a rebuild is forced. This slight delay barely matters for data drives with four parity strips but is more impactful for the three-copy metadata index drives. For example, waiting an hour for data drives “wouldn’t make a significant difference” while just 20 minutes or more on a metadata drive has “extremely high” risk.

    According to recent reports, earlier this year, in May, Micron began shipping the 245 TB 6600 ION, which pulls up to 30 W at maximum load. Kioxia has the LC9, used in a Dell 2U server with 40 drives for a total of 9.8 PB. SanDisk also has its 256 TB UltraQLC, which was due in the first half of this year, and Solidigm is targeting about 245 TB later this year.

    Meanwhile, multiple roadmaps reach petabyte-class drives, including SanDisk’s UltraQLC, a target by SK hynix for QLC SSDs, and Samsung at some time in the future. This strengthens VAST’s case and, while at least the power math adds up, data still needs to be compared openly and fairly to make a firm conclusion about the best pathway forward for what is clearly an unavoidable problem.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.

    Industry observers note that view counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays. But, even with that, YouTube only counts a single view for each time the video is played.

    Now, YouTube notes it might count more views with a new “Co-Views” setup on TVs.

    In a post, YouTube explains that “Co-Views” include “the estimated number of people watching together on TV” in the view count of a video. This only applies to TVs, with views from a mobile device or desktop still only ever counting as a single video. It applies to long-form videos as well as Shorts and Live videos, and only applies going forward – historical data won’t change.

    YouTube states it is making this change to reflect the “over 1 billion hours” spend on YouTube through their TVs “every day” and that the added data will assist creators in channel strategy or brand pitches, while also providing a “more complete picture of how audiences are engaging with’ content, aligning with TV industry standards – including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.” But “Co-Views” won’t count towards earnings on the platform, as they’re not “Qualified Views.”.

    According to recent reports, how is YouTube figuring out what to count here? “Guessing” is not exactly an inaccurate summarization, but Google stresses that it is not using cameras or microphones, but rather a “statistical mode.”.

    Recent findings suggest that youTube doesn’t use devices, cameras, microphones or anything like that. Co-views are estimated using a privacy safe statistical mode, developed by Google research scientists, based on factors like demographic patterns and viewing times, calibrated against ground-truth data sources like industry panels.

    This change is rolling out now.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the same week that Anthropic was floated on the Nasdaq in its initial public offering, a mathematician employed by the organization claims to have discovered proof behind one of the world's most famous math problem, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis.
    • As you're no doubt already aware, and as Alpöge explains, the Riemann Hypothesis is the classic problem in number theory and one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics.
    • As Scientific American notes, the problem is the "North Star for the entire field of number theory, and the most famous open problem in math." Furthermore, the problem was previously thought so insurmountable that experts didn't even bother working on it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the same week that Anthropic was floated on the Nasdaq in its initial public offering, a mathematician employed by the organization claims to have discovered proof behind one of the world's most famous math problem, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis. Levent Alpöge wrote in a paper this week, "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.".

    As you're no doubt already aware, and as Alpöge explains, the Riemann Hypothesis is the classic problem in number theory and one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. Proposed in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, who gave the problem its name, it is the theory that prime numbers are not in fact random but determined. "The Riemann hypothesis asserts that all interesting solutions of the equation ζ(s) = 0 lie on a certain vertical straight line," the Clay Mathematics Institute explains. "This has been checked for the first 10,000,000,000,000 solutions. A proof that it is true for every interesting solution would shed light on many of the mysteries surrounding the distribution of prime numbers.".

    As Scientific American notes, the problem is the "North Star for the entire field of number theory, and the most famous open problem in math." Furthermore, the problem was previously thought so insurmountable that experts didn't even bother working on it.

    Alpöge not only believes that he has used Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, but also believes the method could easily extend to the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, too. "An astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument, far more than I had imagined would be necessary as a student," he writes.

    In a recent development, this would not be the first time that AI has made a significant discovery or finding in a major STEM field. Earlier this year, OpenAI helped create a breakthrough solution for the Navier-Stokes problem, a finding somewhat overshadowed by a plagiarism controversy.

    Alpöge's statement is not without reservation. Aside from confirming whether Claude has actually helped crack the Riemann Hypothesis, which will take some time, he admits sadness at the finding. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.".

    "In a time of revolution in mathematics, I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead," Alpöge adds.

    #92892. Breaking: Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1706 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sitepoint ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
    • Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial.
    • A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

    Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

    Picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

    This happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

    According to recent reports, A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

    Recent findings suggest that the output changes from run to run. If a user claims "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

    Sources indicate that prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt highlights you which one.

    It has been revealed that then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

    So yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

    Recent findings suggest that before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:.

    Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses.

    Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers.

    Passwords, API keys and bearer tokens.

    Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text.

    Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code.

    The first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

    The safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

    Industry observers note that the first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

    According to recent reports, the second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

    Here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

    The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:.

    public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }.

    It has been revealed that nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

    For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:.

    public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = newly introduced LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }.

    According to recent reports, A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

    Regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

    You can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

    Sources indicate that plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email demonstrates up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

    According to recent reports, the fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

    One warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

    In a recent development, free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:.

    log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));.

    Industry observers note that now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

    Industry observers note that streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

    According to recent reports, tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

    Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:.

    Give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

    Sources indicate that limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

    Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

    Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

    Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

    In a recent development, A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:.

    @Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = upcoming RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }.

    Build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a fresh case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

    It has been revealed that A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every new prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

    Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID.

    All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first.

    Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too.

    Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled.

    Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak.

    Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs.

    Good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.
    • Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.
    • With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass new protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block people from filing lawsuits.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.

    Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.

    With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass new protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block people from filing lawsuits.

    On Tuesday, members of a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hosted a hearing calling for the end of forced arbitration for online harms. Their immediate target was Roblox, which they accused of evading legal complaints about children allegedly groomed on the platform by enforcing its own forced arbitration clause against customers who agreed to the terms as minors, in some cases even under the age of 10. Separately, a few blocks away, Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Laurel Lee (R-FL) brought hotel heiress Paris Hilton to Capitol Hill to advocate for the Defiance Act, which would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators.

    “The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), who chairs the Judiciary subcommittee, told reporters after the Roblox hearing. “The more I see these companies evade regulations, the more I think there is nothing as powerful as a jury.” Hawley introduced a fresh bill with ranking member Dick Durbin (D-IL) to render arbitration agreements unenforceable for disputes over alleged child sexual exploitation or “child cyber injury,” which could include “reputational harm, mental suffering,” or death.

    “The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors”.

    Sources indicate that roblox has sought to enforce its arbitration clause in lawsuits it’s facing over allegations that consumers were groomed on the gaming platform as minors, despite the company’s claims of protections. Roblox is facing about 180 lawsuits in a consolidated case over its alleged role in failing to protect children. Under the arbitration process, the public would not get to see legal discovery like the kind that’s come to light under recent cases against Meta. Hawley called the jury system “corruption-proof” and “an incredibly big hammer.”.

    According to recent reports, roblox has denied that it’s trying to dodge accountability. “Safety has been central to Roblox since we released. We require age checks for chat, place people under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” Roblox’s global head of public policy Nicky Jackson Colaço said in a statement. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a manufacturer’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    It has been revealed that congress has only a little more than three more weeks left in session before the end of the year, and a new Democratic majority will be sworn in come January. Republicans are expected to do their best to push through President Donald Trump’s nominees for judgeships and executive branch posts like FCC commissioner in the lame-duck session, as well as try to pass year-end bills like the National Defense Authorization Act, which often includes a range of other policy items. But some lawmakers are holding out hope that they can open up courthouses to new litigation over deepfake abuse and child predation.

    Sources indicate that litigation has become one of the more successful ways for survivors of online harm to seek change. Congress has failed to pass many prominent child safety, privacy, and consumer protection bills, though it has begun to tackle the deepfake concern through the Take It Down Act. At the same time, attorneys general and individual plaintiffs have collected significant settlements and legal wins despite the broad scope of tech’s legal shield, Section 230. If bills like the Defiance Act or those seeking to end forced arbitration were to pass, tech companies and perpetrators of online harms could become vulnerable to a fresh wave of legal challenges.

    “You will be amazed by how swiftly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court”.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to Hawley and Durbin’s bill about forced arbitration, Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Katie Britt (R-AL), and Cory Booker (D-NJ) introduced a similar bill with a slightly different approach, including explicitly covering data privacy violations. At the Roblox hearing, Northwestern University law professor Myriam Gilles, an expert on forced arbitration, said she’s testified before Congress many times on this topic, but “never expected to come before this body to talk about its use against 9 year olds.” Passing either proposal, she said, would have a profound impact. “You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court.”.

    Industry observers note that the Defiance Act would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators for damages, in an attempt to raise the cost of creating these kinds of images. Hilton visited Washington earlier this year to share how an intimate non-deepfake video of her at age 19 shared without her consent impacted her life, and she used her story to advocate for the Defiance Act. At Tuesday’s press conference, she stated she would come back to Congress as many times as necessary for the bill to become law. “Some people might have thought that was the end of my fight,” Hilton said. “But when I make a promise to survivors, I keep it.”.

    Hilton said over 50 million people have been victimized by sexually explicit deepfakes. “For me personally, strangers have created over 100,000 AI-generated explicit images and videos portraying me in the most graphic and disturbing ways imaginable,” Hilton said. “If this can happen to someone with my resources and my platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone.”.

    Industry observers note that hilton’s comments were followed by Elliston Berry, an advocate who stated a classmate made an explicit deepfake image of her friend group “from an innocent social media post” when she was 14, and distributed it throughout her school. “In a matter of seconds, my sense of security disappeared,” she said. “For me, the Defiance Act means recognition that victims deserve to be heard, that their experience matters, and that their right to seek justice should not depend on how quickly technology advances.”.

A decent one can easily cost $1,000 if not $2,000 now. But it looks like Lenovo might be about to announce a relatively cheap handheld once again— the Legion Go Beam.

    Windows Latest has leaked images of the handheld, and there’s no question it’s designed to be a value alternative to even the tech giant’s least expensive Legion Go S variant. While it’s got the same big stippled grips and triggers for comfort, there’s only one USB-C port on the top instead of two, a comparatively cheap-looking D-pad, no touchpad, and only a single tiny intake and exhaust for its fan.

    There’s no SteamOS logo where that would go, so it likely runs Windows instead… but then there’s that name, “Beam.” Perhaps you’ll “beam” your games to it because it’s a streaming and cloud gaming handheld, instead of one that primarily plays games on its own chip? Maybe that’s why it doesn’t need as much airflow as previous handhelds?

    Perhaps there’s a partnership with Xbox Cloud Gaming specifically, and that’s why it’s all lit up in Xbox green?

    Industry observers note that but it might just be green because it looks nice with white, which has been the “value” color for handhelds so far (see: ROG Ally, Xbox Ally, and the Windows-based Legion Go S). And it might be “Beam” because there’s a literal beam of light on the bottom, even though the first thing I do with most handhelds is turn any and all distracting RGB lighting off. Or maybe it’s “Beam” just because it sounds like a friendly, fun, value-oriented name, instead of something “S” or “Pro.”.

    I won’t begin to speculate on the Legion Go Beam’s price, except to say that “cheap” may be relative. The Legion Go S was originally supposed to cost $499, but wound up costing far more except on the occasional sale. The Legion Go 2 was supposed to start at $1,099 but wound up costing $1,500 and up after RAMageddon. Streaming-first handhelds have been far cheaper, though, like the $249 Sony PlayStation Portal.

    Lenovo has a history of announcing its upcoming gaming devices at CES in January each year, including previous Legion Go handhelds, so I’m expecting to see an official announcement of the Lenovo Legion Go Beam then. Even if so, that doesn’t mean it’ll be available in January — there’s often a many-month lag.

    Breaking: Grand Theft Auto VI understands just how important a smartphone is

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.
    • Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.
    • According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto VI, in many ways, tries to simulate real life.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.

    Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.

    According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto VI, in many ways, tries to simulate real life. And life in 2026 would not be complete without a smartphone. GTA VI understands this and makes the phone not just a central part of the experience, but an object that exists within the world. You may try to escape into a fantasy of robbing banks and fighting drug lords, but you can’t get away from texts from your mom or nagging fitness app notifications.

    Seeing a smartphone in a game isn’t a new phenomenon. The device has become a natural stand-in for the main menu in many games, giving players an interface that feels intuitive, because a phone is something they use every day. But the phone in GTA VI is different for a few reasons. One is that it behaves much like any other object in the game, whether it’s a gun or a bottle of beer. The action doesn’t pause when you use your phone. Instead, the game switches to a first-person viewpoint, where you can still walk around — or drive, if you’re feeling ambitious — while reading texts or flipping through a fictional version of Instagram.

    Rob Nelson, the co-studio head at developer Rockstar North and producer on GTA VI, says that it would’ve felt “archaic” to have a static phone that worked like those in other games, or the one in GTA V, which appeared as a pop-up at the bottom of the screen across from the minimap. “We felt that it was key to make it physical so you have to look at it and put your attention on it, including while driving,” he explains. “It’s about finding the line between realism and player convenience. But the act of being lost in your phone felt like something worth doing, even though it could mean slightly more inconvenience. In this game you are committing to using it.” (Of course, texting and driving, like much of what you do in GTA VI, is both very dangerous and very illegal.).

    It has been revealed that you have to interact with the phone in the game constantly. Often the story plays out through phone calls and text messages, and you have a surprisingly large array of apps to use that serve a real purpose in the game. You manage your money in a banking app, use a rideshare app when you need a lift, track your workouts in a fitness app, scroll through a social network complete with comments and the ability to like posts, and sideload an AI tool that scans nearby cars so you can see how easy they’ll be to steal. You can even change the wallpaper and ringtone. (GTA VI has two main characters that you swap between, and each has their own phone, though they’re functionally identical.).

    In a recent development, what’s most impressive is how all of these apps interact with each other. For instance, after pulling off a major heist, a friend might text you a news story about it, asking “was this you!?” You can then click the link, open up the news app, and read an actual article about what went down. These kinds of interactions can be functional, like when another character texts you a location, which you can then add to your map so the GPS can guide you there. Other times, they add texture to the world or depth to the characters. GTA VI is a love story about two criminals named Jason and Lucia, and you play as both. At one point, while controlling Lucia, I got a text asking for a selfie. I opened up the camera, shot a pic of Lucia drinking a latte, and sent it over. Jason replied immediately — and their relationship got a boost.

    It has been revealed that phones are so fully integrated into the game that they can even interrupt the characters’ sleep. At the end of each day, you can click on a bed to rest for the night. But neither Jason nor Lucia will instantly fall asleep when you do — instead, they’ll sit down and pull out their phone, and you have the option to doomscroll or catch up on texts instead of going to sleep right away. Nelson indicates that this was implemented because the developers wanted to include the ability for the characters to sit on the bed at night, much like a real couple in a shared living space might do. “We needed something to do aside from just sitting there staring at nothing,” he says.

    It has been revealed that if nothing else, GTA VI’s phone shows how alike we all are: Even bank robbers being hunted by the police can’t seem to stop scrolling. “Phones are a constant part of our lives,” Nelson claims of the evolution, “even more than they were in 2013.”.

    A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report reveals two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

    Both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

    Industry observers note that A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

    This tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

    Before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a newly introduced purchase.

    Use separate identifiers for these different things:.

    Recent findings suggest that this separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

    In a recent development, for this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

    According to recent reports, keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

    Industry observers note that campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

    Google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:.
